dauBookings.title: DAU vs Bookings growth
dauBookings.content:
Bookings is cash collected for subscriptions and in-app purchases in the period (recognised as revenue over the following months as usage occurs). DAU is daily active users.

For Duolingo, Inc.: bookings growth has decelerated sharply while DAU growth has stayed strong -- Q2 2026 bookings were +8% YoY against +23% DAU growth, and FY2026 guidance holds bookings to +10-12% against 20%+ DAU growth. Management attributes the gap to the Max-tier subscription sunset compressing ARPU as users shift into lower-priced tiers; if the gap persists rather than closes, it breaks the historical bookings-to-DAU conversion the valuation is built on.

What to watch:

  • Whether the DAU-bookings gap narrows or keeps widening quarter over quarter
  • Currency: over 50% of bookings are ex-US, so USD strength is a second headwind
  • Revenue lags bookings by roughly five months through deferred revenue, so today's bookings deceleration is next year's revenue print

bookings.title: Bookings
bookings.content:
Bookings is cash collected in the period for subscriptions and a la carte purchases, before deferral; subscription bookings is the recurring-revenue slice of it. Revenue is recognised later as the underlying service is delivered, so it lags bookings.

For Duolingo, Inc.: bookings is the leading indicator revenue will follow in ~5 months via the deferred-revenue balance; it decelerated from 33% growth to a 10-12% FY2026 guided range even as revenue growth has stayed in the mid-teens to date, so the revenue line here is the trailing half of the same story.

What to watch:

  • Bookings growth relative to the FY2026 10-12% guide
  • Subscription bookings as a share of total (Max/Super mix shift)
  • The gap between bookings growth and revenue growth closing as deferred revenue runs off

users.title: Daily and monthly active users
users.content:
DAU is daily active users; MAU is monthly active users. DAU/MAU (not charted separately) is a stickiness ratio.

For Duolingo, Inc.: DAU growth (+23% YoY in Q2 2026) is the strongest engagement metric in the business and the counter-argument to the bookings slowdown -- the bull case is that this base eventually converts to bookings once the Max-tier pricing transition laps.

What to watch:

  • DAU growth holding up while bookings growth falls (the current pattern)
  • DAU/MAU ratio for engagement depth, not just reach

subscribers.title: Paid subscribers
subscribers.content:
Subscribers is the paid subscriber base across all tiers (Super, Max, families).

For Duolingo, Inc.: subscriber count growing while subscription bookings decelerate is consistent with management's explanation -- users converting into lower-ARPU tiers as Max is folded into Super, which is the mechanism behind the bookings/DAU divergence above.

What to watch:

  • Subscriber growth vs. subscription bookings growth (ARPU direction)
  • Paid conversion rate against the DAU base

balanceSheet.title: Balance sheet
balanceSheet.content:
Shareholders' equity is assets less liabilities; plotted against total liabilities to show leverage.

For Duolingo, Inc.: equity that grows only through revaluations or share issues is not the same as retained earnings.

What to watch:

  • Liabilities growing faster than equity
  • Goodwill share of equity after acquisitions

cashDebt.title: Cash and debt
cashDebt.content:
Cash & equivalents against total borrowings (leases excluded unless noted).

For Duolingo, Inc.: the DCF's net-debt bridge uses these balances at the latest balance-sheet date.

What to watch:

  • Net debt trend versus EBITDA
  • Refinancing dates and covenants in the filings

ebitda.title: EBITDA
ebitda.content:
EBITDA is earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation -- an operating-cash proxy that ignores capital intensity.

For Duolingo, Inc.: read it beside CapEx: a business that must reinvest most of its EBITDA is not as cash-generative as the margin suggests.

What to watch:

  • EBITDA margin trend
  • Gap between EBITDA and operating cash flow (working capital)

epsDps.title: EPS and dividends
epsDps.content:
EPS is net income per share; DPS is the cash dividend paid per share. Both are in major currency units.

For Duolingo, Inc.: the payout ratio (DPS / EPS) shows how much of earnings is returned versus reinvested.

What to watch:

  • EPS growth versus net income growth (dilution)
  • Dividends funded from earnings, not debt

fcf.title: Free cash flow
fcf.content:
Reported FCF is operating cash flow less capital expenditure. Owner FCF (from the DCF) further deducts stock-based compensation, interest income and lease principal -- the cash an owner could actually take out.

For Duolingo, Inc.: the gap between net income and owner FCF is the earnings-quality question the valuation is built on.

What to watch:

  • FCF persistently below net income
  • Working-capital swings inflating one year's FCF

margins.title: Margins
margins.content:
Gross margin is revenue less cost of revenue; operating margin deducts operating expenses; net margin is after interest and tax.

For Duolingo, Inc.: the spread between gross and operating margin is the cost of running the business; a widening spread with flat gross margin means opex is growing faster than sales.

What to watch:

  • Direction of operating margin over several years, not one
  • One-offs (impairments, disposals) that distort net margin

ocfCapex.title: Operating cash flow and CapEx
ocfCapex.content:
Operating cash flow is cash generated by operations; CapEx is cash invested in fixed and intangible assets.

For Duolingo, Inc.: CapEx here is shown as stored (sign convention varies by ticker); the DCF splits it into stay-in-business and growth where disclosed.

What to watch:

  • CapEx rising faster than revenue
  • OCF that diverges from EBITDA

profit.title: Profit lines
profit.content:
Gross profit is revenue less cost of revenue; operating income deducts operating expenses; net income is after interest, tax and one-offs.

For Duolingo, Inc.: the three lines together show where margin is made and lost between the top line and the bottom.

What to watch:

  • Operating income growing slower than gross profit (opex creep)
  • Net income far from operating income (interest, tax, one-offs)

revenue.title: Revenue
revenue.content:
Revenue is the top line: what customers paid for goods and services in the period, before any costs.

For Duolingo, Inc.: the growth rate matters more than the level; compare it with the DCF's base-case growth path below.

What to watch:

  • Acceleration or deceleration in YoY growth
  • Whether growth is organic or acquired
  • Interim rows show seasonality

sbc.title: Stock-based compensation and share count
sbc.content:
Stock-based comp is the expense of equity awards; shares outstanding shows the dilution it causes net of buybacks.

For Duolingo, Inc.: the DCF charges SBC as a cash cost and holds the share count flat, so this chart is the check on that assumption.

What to watch:

  • Share count rising while buybacks are advertised
  • SBC as a percentage of revenue
